# Cultural shifts

## Authors

- Bridget M Kuehn<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0001-8783-4419](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-8783-4419)) †

### Affiliations

1. eLife Chicago United States

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

China’s one-child policy has resulted in scientists with families having experiences that are very different to those elsewhere in the world.

## Changing times and countries

Ling-An Wu, an emeritus professor of physics at the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Beijing, has lived through many of these changes. Her two sons were born just before the one-child policy came into effect, when good childcare centers were free and plentiful. This allowed her to work as an English translator and interpreter. “I was really lucky in that respect,” she says. Wu also benefited from a supportive husband who, like many men in the urban areas of China, shared the household duties.

The ‘Cultural Revolution’ had previously put her studies on hold but in 1981 at the age of 37, she was given the chance to pursue graduate studies in the US. With support from her mother and a nanny, who helped to look after her children who stayed in China, Wu was able to complete a PhD at the University of Texas at Austin. “It was my mother who said I should go to make up for what I lost during the Cultural Revolution,” recalls Wu. “I am really grateful to her.”

Now, younger Chinese women are grappling with a new set of challenges and opportunities. Like Wu, Nan Tang, an assistant investigator at the National Institute of Biological Sciences (NIBS) in Beijing, spent time in the US as a scientist parent. Her son Haikun Du was born when she was a postdoc working on embryonic lung development at the University of California, San Francisco. Many of her peers at UCSF were also having children so she was able to swap stories with them about getting pregnant or caring for a newborn.

“It was very, very supportive,” she says. That support helped to lessen her worries that having a child would slow down her career and got her through a tough bout of morning sickness during her first four months of pregnancy. Having health insurance through the university also proved crucial when she experienced a complication during delivery: “The medical bill was huge.”

Tang and her husband decided on a childcare center near his office, which meant that she spent more than an hour each way commuting to and from work on public transport every day. But she quickly learned to make the most of this time, using it to read and deal with emails. This allowed her to focus on her bench work and collaborations while she was in the office.

“I found I was more efficient at work,” says Tang. She also received a lot of support from her husband, who worked for a technology company: “Not only for science, but for every career you need support from the other side. I support him and at the same time he supports me.”

## On the baby bus

Tang moved back to China for her current position at NIBS in 2012. The institute recruits many junior principal investigators from the United States and other countries, and has strong systems in place for supporting parents. “They try to make the transition as smooth as they can,” she says. For example, the institute rented an apartment for Tang and her family before they arrived, and it helped to get her son enrolled in an elementary school.

Tang and her husband chose to send her son to an elementary school close to her husband's work. Most investigators send their children to another elementary school that is about six miles away from the institute. Children who attend this school ride what investigators affectionately refer to as the ‘baby shuttle’. Every morning the shuttle driver picks up the children from home and drives them to school; then, in the afternoon, he drives them from school to the institute so that they can go home with their parents.

![Figure](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/37432/elife-37432-fig1-v1.jpg)

All women in China are entitled to at least 98 days of maternity leave, and some employers offer more: Chunni Zhang, for example, has just finished a four-month maternity leave from Peking University. However, after the mother has returned to work it can be challenging to find childcare for children who are too young to go to school. In the past new parents often relied on grandparents for childcare, but many new parents – especially academics – now live far from their families. “This puts a lot of pressure on young couples,” says Zhang, particularly because the demand for childcare centers has exceeded supply since the one-child policy was relaxed. Ling-An Wu agrees that more childcare centres are needed.

Wu has experience enacting change. In 2000, after she had established herself as a researcher in China, she joined an international working group on women in physics. She was shocked to find that the number of women in physics in China was declining, particularly at the senior level. “I thought men and women had equal opportunities,” Wu says. “It was true for decades.”

She and the working group lobbied the National Natural Science Foundation, one of the biggest funding agencies in China, to extend the age limit for women applying for certain grants in physics from 35 to 38 to account for career breaks to raise children. She was pleasantly surprised when the foundation agreed to raise the age limit to 40 for women in all science disciplines. “It takes time to change the mindset, particularly of men,” says Wu. “You have to convince them there is a problem.”

## Sharing in science

Being a parent and a scientist requires hard work and organization, but Nan Tang thinks it is well worth it. She sometimes gets to teach her nine-year-old son and his classmates through a volunteer program at school. She also gets to share in his growing love of science, which includes dinosaurs and astronauts.

“Being a parent is the best thing in the world but being a scientist also is the best thing, I love my work,” Tang says. “It is so much fun to be a scientist.”

## Note

This Feature Article is part of the Scientist and Parent collection.

results.result: Ling-An Wu's experience as a scientist-parent in China before and during the one-child policy era demonstrates how free childcare, supportive family structures, and spousal support enabled her career progression despite the Cultural Revolution interrupting her education. Wu had two sons just before the one-child policy, benefited from free childcare centers and a supportive husband, and later completed a PhD in the US at age 37 with family support for childcare.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C11 provide consistent biographical information about Wu's career and family life, including verifiable facts (her position, timing of children, PhD completion) and her own testimony about family support. These are straightforward factual claims about one individual's experience that are internally consistent and supported by direct quotes.

results.result: Nan Tang's experience as a postdoc parent at UCSF illustrates how institutional support (health insurance, peer support) and personal strategies (commute time management, spousal support) enabled her to maintain research productivity while raising a child. Tang had her son during her postdoc, received crucial health insurance coverage for delivery complications, developed efficient time management strategies, and reported increased work efficiency after becoming a parent.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C26 provide a coherent narrative of Tang's experience at UCSF with specific details about her research, childcare arrangements, commute, and support systems. The claims are internally consistent and include direct quotes from Tang herself, though they represent subjective assessments of efficiency (C25) alongside factual details.

results.result: NIBS in Beijing provides comprehensive institutional support for scientist-parents, including housing assistance, school enrollment help, and a 'baby shuttle' transportation system that facilitates work-life balance for investigators with children. Tang returned to NIBS in 2012 and benefited from these support systems, though she chose a different school arrangement than most investigators.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C36 describe specific institutional support mechanisms at NIBS with concrete details (apartment rental, school enrollment assistance, shuttle service logistics). These are verifiable institutional practices corroborated by Tang's direct experience (C30-C31) and observable patterns among other investigators (C33-C36).

results.result: Current childcare challenges in China stem from changing family structures and policy shifts. While maternity leave is mandated (minimum 98 days), the relaxation of the one-child policy has created childcare shortages, and geographic mobility of academics has reduced traditional grandparent-based childcare, creating pressure on young scientist-parents.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C39 about maternity leave are verifiable policy facts, but claims C40-C44 about childcare challenges rely on anecdotal evidence from Zhang and general assertions without quantitative data on supply-demand imbalances or systematic evidence of geographic mobility patterns among academics. The causal link between policy relaxation and childcare shortages (C44) lacks supporting data.

results.result: Wu's advocacy work led to successful policy change at China's National Natural Science Foundation, extending the age limit for women applying for grants from 35 to 40 across all science disciplines to account for career breaks for childrearing. This was prompted by Wu's discovery of declining representation of women in physics, particularly at senior levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C53 describe a clear advocacy effort with a documented outcome (age limit extension to 40). The policy change is a verifiable institutional action by a major funding agency (C51, C53), though the claim about declining women's representation (C48) lacks quantitative evidence and relies on Wu's observation through the working group.

results.result: Tang's current experience demonstrates successful integration of parenting and scientific career, with her son developing scientific interests and Tang maintaining enthusiasm for both roles. She engages in volunteer teaching and views the dual role as rewarding despite requiring hard work and organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C60 provide consistent information about Tang's current situation with specific details (son's age, volunteer activities, his interests) and direct quotes expressing her positive assessment. These are straightforward factual and testimonial claims about one individual's experience and perspective.

results.result: The overarching thesis that China's one-child policy resulted in scientists with families having experiences very different from those elsewhere in the world.
results.evaluation: Claim C1 is the main thesis but is marked as speculation (evidence_type). While the article provides detailed accounts of individual experiences (Wu, Tang, Zhang), it lacks comparative data with scientists in other countries, systematic analysis of how experiences differ, or evidence that the one-child policy specifically (rather than other factors like economic development, institutional structures, or cultural norms) caused these differences. The narrative is illustrative but not conclusive for the broad comparative claim.
